bib.venue: book chapter (O'Reilly, per file path; not printed)

question: How can we learn low-dimensional embeddings without labels, by autoencoders when the input is rich and by context prediction (Word2Vec Skip-Gram) when the context carries the information?
hypothesis: Nonlinear neural autoencoders capture structure that linear PCA misses (Hinton and Salakhutdinov 2006).
contributions: PCA and its failure on nonlinear data
Feed-forward autoencoder on MNIST vs PCA in TensorFlow
Word2Vec CBOW and Skip-Gram with NCE, implemented in TensorFlow

results.claim: A 2-D-code autoencoder reaches validation L2 reconstruction cost 4.78 on MNIST after about 200 epochs.
results.source: Cost is sqrt of summed squares averaged over minibatch (not MSE).
results.metric: mean per-image L2 distance (784-d) on validation set
results.setup: MNIST, feed-forward sigmoid autoencoder with batch norm, Adam lr 0.001, 2-neuron code layer unless stated
results.quote: cost of 4.78, our autoencoder is producing high-quality reconstructions.

results.claim: Yardstick for that cost: a chosen image of a 1 is on average 5.75 L2 units from other 1s in MNIST.
results.setup: MNIST, one arbitrary image X of a 1 vs every image of each class
results.quote: On average, X is 5.75 units away from other 1’s in MNIST.

results.claim: Nearest non-1 class to X is 7s at 8.94 L2 units.
results.quote: the non-1 digits closest to the X are the 7’s (8.94 units)

results.claim: Farthest class from X is 0s at 11.05 L2 units.
Qualitatively the 2-D autoencoder beats 2-D PCA: PCA confuses 5/3/8, 0/8, 4/9 and resembles the autoencoder after only 5 epochs; autoencoder 2-D codes cluster by digit while PCA codes do not.
results.setup: MNIST test images, 2-D codes, Figs 6-10 and 6-11; no number reported
results.quote: it’s quite clear that the autoencoder vastly outperforms PCA with two-dimensional codes.

results.claim: With 30-dimensional codes PCA improves a lot but is still significantly worse than the 30-d autoencoder (no numbers given).
results.quote: Repeating the same experiment with 30-dimensional codes

results.setup: Skip-Gram with NCE, corpus not named
results.quote: we employ a minibatch size of 32 examples and train for 5 epochs

results.claim: Skip-Gram trained with plain SGD at learning rate 0.1.
results.quote: employ stochastic gradient descent with a learning rate of 0.1

results.claim: NCE uses 64 randomly chosen non-context words.

Validation: 20 random words from the 500 most common of a 10,000-word vocabulary, nearest neighbours by cosine similarity; neighbours are qualitatively sensible (white: yellow, black, red; eight: six, seven, five).
results.quote: We randomly select 20 validation words out of the 500 most common

results.claim: PCA keeps top-m eigenvectors of the covariance matrix and fails on nonlinear structure such as two concentric circles (equal variance in all directions).
results.quote: there is no linear direction that contains more information here than another (we have equal variance in all directions)

results.claim: Denoising autoencoder: zero a fixed fraction of input pixels, encoder sees corrupted input, target is the clean image; the corruption in the code zeroes about half the pixels.
results.setup: MNIST; corrupt_input draws uniform ints in {0,1} so each pixel is kept with p=0.5
results.quote: We corrupt some fixed percentage of the pixels in the input image by setting them to zero.

results.claim: Sparsity: add beta times a sparsity penalty (KL divergence against a zero-mean target) to the loss; k-sparse autoencoders (Makhzani and Frey 2013/2014) were shown as effective as other sparsity mechanisms and cheaper.
results.source: Makhzani and Frey, k-Sparse Autoencoders, arXiv:1312.5663
results.quote: These k-Sparse autoencoders were shown to be just as effective as other mechanisms of sparsity
results.note: Cited as 2013 in footnote 6 and 2014 in text.

results.claim: CBOW works best for smaller datasets; Skip-Gram is the inverse (target word predicts a context word).
results.quote: It turns out this strategy works

limits: Code is Python 2 and TensorFlow 0.x (tf.sub, tf.scalar_summary, xrange, print statements); dated.
Autoencoder encoder() function is never printed; hidden sizes (n_decoder_hidden_1..3), batch size and training_epochs are not stated.
Embedding comparison with PCA is visual; no downstream classifier accuracy is reported.
Skip-Gram corpus is not named; 10,000-word vocabulary only.
NCE is described as summing probabilities of noise and subtracting the context probability (optimum -1), a simplified account, not the standard NCE/negative-sampling loss.
Sparsity section gives no implementation or results.
The PCA formula is garbled in the text layer ('T = X').
practices: Use ReLU normally but sigmoid in autoencoders when the codes will be visualised, to avoid sharp transitions (p.123).
Reuse batch normalization to speed autoencoder training (p.123).
Monitor train and validation L2 cost and compare against inter-class L2 distances to judge whether a cost is good (p.127-129).
Use denoising (corrupt input, reconstruct clean) as regularisation for robust codes (p.134).
Add a sparsity penalty when the code layer is as large as the input, otherwise the net can learn a copy operation (p.139).
Use Word2Vec embeddings instead of one-hot vectors for language models (p.146).
Initialise embedding matrix uniform in [-1, 1]; inspect with cosine-similarity nearest neighbours; visualise with t-SNE (p.146-151).
